teaser: Two people serve dinner to a man who died three days ago. Only the guests have understood.
review_notes:
IMAGE/METADATA MISMATCH: the image is Caravaggio's SECOND Supper at Emmaus (1606, Pinacoteca di Brera, Milan: bearded Christ, old woman servant, no fruit basket), not the 1601 National Gallery, London version named in the catalog. The lesson describes the picture actually shown and says so; fix either the image or the title/year/museum. If the image is swapped for the London painting, this lesson must be rewritten.
Painted in summer 1606 on the Colonna estates south of Rome after the killing of Ranuccio Tomassoni (28 May 1606).
In the Patrizi collection in Rome by the 1620s; acquired by the Brera in 1939.
Size about 141 x 175 cm.
The dish carried by the old woman is usually described as lamb.
Papal pardon reportedly on its way when Caravaggio died in July 1610.

lesson.text: Five people share this table and they are not living the same evening. For three of them the world has just turned over. For the two standing behind, it is a slow night at the inn and a customer is saying grace over his bread. The miracle and the routine sit a few inches apart, in one pool of light.

The Gospel of Luke tells it this way. Three days after the crucifixion, two disciples walk to the village of Emmaus. A stranger joins them on the road and they invite him to supper. When he blesses and breaks the bread, they suddenly know him: it is Jesus, alive. A moment later he is gone.

Caravaggio painted this scene twice. The first, from 1601, is the famous one in London: bright color, a young beardless Christ, arms flung wide, a fruit basket about to tip off the table. The picture in front of you is the second, made five years later and now in Milan. Almost everything has been turned down.

In May 1606 Caravaggio killed a man named Ranuccio Tomassoni in a street fight in Rome and fled with a death sentence on his head. He hid on the estates of the Colonna family in the hills south of the city. This Supper was painted there, within weeks.

You can feel the change of circumstances in the paint itself. It is thin and quick. In the shadows he lets the dark brown undercoat stand in for whole areas, and the palette shrinks to earth colors and one muted green. With so little to look at, the story has to be carried by something else: hands.

lesson.title: Four pairs of hands
lesson.text: Go around the table. Each person's hands say how much they have understood.

spots.title: The blessing
spots.text: Christ raises two fingers over the bread, a small gesture held close to the body. His eyes are lowered and half his face is in shadow. He seems already on the point of leaving.

spots.title: An open palm
spots.text: The disciple with his back to us lifts a hand off the table, fingers spread. We cannot see his face, so this startled hand is his whole reaction.

spots.title: Holding on
spots.text: The other disciple presses one hand on the tablecloth near Christ's and grips the table edge with the other, leaning in hard, as if the furniture might steady him.

spots.title: The dish
spots.text: The old woman holds a plate of meat with both hands and looks down at it. She is thinking about serving. Whatever is happening at the table has not reached her.

lesson.text: Next to her, the innkeeper frowns down at his guest, puzzled but not moved. Caravaggio gives these two the best-lit faces in the picture, every wrinkle recorded. It is a pointed choice. The people who see most clearly, in the plain sense, are the ones who miss it.
In the first Emmaus, astonishment is a big gesture. In the second, it is a held breath. Caravaggio found that he could say more with less movement, less color and less light.

The table shows the same economy. Where the London version piled up a still life, meaning a display of painted objects such as food and dishes, this one offers a meal you could count on one hand. Spend some time among the few things he kept.

spots.title: The broken bread
spots.text: A roll already split open, lying on a dish with a few green leaves. This is the moment the Gospel names: they knew him in the breaking of the bread.

spots.title: A second loaf
spots.text: Whole and untouched, at the near edge of the cloth. Its crust is painted with a few thick strokes of ocher over the dark ground.

spots.title: The jug
spots.text: A pottery pitcher with a painted pattern, the kind found in any country kitchen. A streak of white along its side is all the shine Caravaggio allows himself.

spots.title: The innkeeper
spots.text: Cap on his head, forehead creased, he looks at Christ without a trace of recognition. His face is weathered and specific, clearly a real person who posed.

spots.title: The old woman
spots.text: Deep-set eyes, sunken cheeks, a neck like cord. She is new: the London picture had no such figure. Her tired face sets the mood of the whole scene.

spots.title: Christ's face
spots.text: Bearded now, older and worn, eyes cast down. One side is lit, the other disappears. The triumphant young man of 1601 has become someone you might not recognize either.

lesson.text: The canvas soon belonged to the Patrizi family in Rome and stayed with them for about three centuries. The Brera gallery in Milan bought it in 1939.

Caravaggio never returned to Rome. He spent four years moving between Naples, Malta and Sicily, painting darker and sparer pictures, and died in 1610 on his way back, with a pardon reportedly on its way. So what changed between the two Suppers: his idea of the story, or the man holding the brush?

quiz.question: How do the two disciples recognize Jesus in the Gospel story?
options: By the wounds in his hands
When he blesses and breaks the bread
quiz.explanation: Luke says they knew him in the breaking of the bread.

quiz.question: What had happened shortly before Caravaggio painted this second version?
options: He had killed a man and fled Rome
He had been made a knight in Malta
quiz.explanation: He painted it in hiding after killing Ranuccio Tomassoni in May 1606.

quiz.question: Which figure appears here but not in the earlier London version?
options: The old woman carrying a dish
quiz.explanation: The old servant woman is new in the second version.

quiz.question: How do the innkeeper and the old woman react?
quiz.explanation: He frowns, puzzled, and she looks at her dish: the miracle has not reached them.

quiz.question: Compared with the first version, this painting is...
options: Brighter and more crowded with objects
quiz.explanation: Color, gesture and still life are all reduced.

facts.text: Christ is shown with a beard in this second version.
facts.explanation: Here he is bearded and worn; in the 1601 version he was young and beardless.

facts.text: The table is loaded with a large basket of fruit.
facts.explanation: That belongs to the first version; here there is only bread, a dish and a jug.

facts.text: Caravaggio painted this picture while hiding on the Colonna family estates.
facts.explanation: He had fled Rome after the killing and worked there in the summer of 1606.
